questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: State what an LD50 establishes about a substance and what it does not.
questions.stem: Memo to committee: a new paint stripper's safety data sheet reports an oral LD50 of 240 mg per kg in rats, and I must advise what that means.

options.text: The dose that is safe for everyday use, so the site's public exposure limit can be taken from it directly.
options.misconception: treats an LD50 as a safe human exposure limit

options.text: The dose at which half the people tested died, which is exactly the dose the public will experience.
options.misconception: confuses animal test doses with human exposure

options.text: The dose that kills half the test rats, which is a hazard measure and says nothing about the doses people meet.
The lowest dose that caused any death, which is a conservative figure for regulating the site.
options.misconception: believes LD50 means the lowest lethal dose

questions.explanation: An LD50 is the dose killing 50 percent of a defined test population by a defined route, so it measures laboratory potency, not real-world risk. It is neither a safe dose nor the lowest lethal dose.
questions.hint: Hazard, not exposure, and not a safety limit.

questions.topic: From a no-effect level to an intake limit
questions.learningObjective: Derive a working intake limit from a no-effect level.
questions.stem: Memo: the toxicology report gives a no observed adverse effect level of 0.5 mg per kg of body weight per day for the compound.

options.text: Use the no-effect level directly, since it is the highest dose with no effects in the study.
options.misconception: treats a no-effect level as a safe limit

options.text: Divide the no-effect level by an uncertainty factor of 100, giving 0.005 mg per kg per day.
Multiply the no-effect level by a safety factor of ten, giving a limit five times higher.
options.misconception: applies safety factors in the wrong direction

options.text: Set the limit at one hundredth of the lowest dose that caused harm, the strictest option available.
options.misconception: confuses a lowest effect level with a no-effect level

questions.explanation: A no-effect level is a study observation, so dividing it by an uncertainty factor of 100 gives a working limit of 0.005 mg per kg per day. Multiplying raises the limit, and a lowest effect level is another quantity.
questions.hint: Divide by a factor that covers the uncertainty.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a bioconcentration factor from paired water and tissue concentrations.
questions.stem: Memo: water upstream of the site holds 0.008 mg per litre, and fish in the downstream pool hold 0.04 mg per kg of whole body.
questions.explanation: The bioconcentration factor is the organism's steady-state concentration over the water concentration: 0.04 over 0.008 is 5 litres per kilogram. It covers uptake from water alone, not diet or sediment.
questions.hint: Steady state, water to organism.

options.text: A log value that high flags high potential to accumulate in fatty tissue, so further testing is warranted.
A log value that high means the compound is insoluble in water and so cannot reach the site.
options.misconception: confuses low water solubility with absence of exposure

options.text: A log value that high shows the compound will bioaccumulate, so no further testing is needed.
options.misconception: treats a screening value as a measured result

options.text: A log value that high means the compound is metabolised rapidly and will not persist in fish.
options.misconception: assumes lipophilicity indicates fast metabolism

questions.explanation: A high log partition coefficient flags a tendency to concentrate in lipid, so it justifies testing but cannot replace a measured study. Solubility, metabolism and ionisation modify the outcome.
questions.hint: A screen flags risk; it does not settle it.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how persistence and a continuing source produce a standing concentration.
questions.stem: Memo: a former drum store on the site still shows a solvent plume, and I need to explain how the concentration behaves.

options.text: Concentration falls linearly to zero in a fixed time, because the solvent evaporates at a steady rate.
options.misconception: assumes linear rather than exponential decline

options.text: Concentration stays constant until the source is removed, since decay does not start before clean-up.
options.misconception: assumes decay waits for source removal

options.text: Concentration falls faster in early months then slows, because the plume is diluted as it spreads.
options.misconception: attributes the tail to dilution rather than kinetics

options.text: Concentration follows first-order decay, so each half-life cuts the level in half and a source keeps a standing plume.

questions.explanation: First-order decay is exponential, so a 30-day half-life halves the concentration every 30 days, giving a long tail while the source continues. Decay starts at once, and dilution does not change the decay rate.
questions.hint: Half-lives multiply, they do not add.

questions.learningObjective: Plan a route-to-route conversion for an inhalation assessment.
questions.stem: Memo: the only animal study used oral dosing, and the committee wants an inhalation figure for workers on the site.

answer.exemplar: The plan converts the oral dose into an absorbed dose using the gastrointestinal absorption fraction, then divides that systemic dose by the lung absorption fraction to obtain the inhaled dose delivering the same internal exposure. It should state the uncertainty factors applied and flag that metabolism may differ between routes.

questions.explanation: A good answer converts oral dose to absorbed dose using gastrointestinal uptake, then back-calculates the inhaled dose for the same internal exposure, with uncertainty stated. Comparing masses alone is not enough.
questions.hint: Absorbed dose is the common currency.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish hazard from exposure in a site risk statement.
questions.stem: Memo: the committee wants to know whether the solvent on the site is dangerous, and my file holds a toxicity study and site conditions.

options.text: The toxicity study settles it, because a hazardous substance is dangerous wherever it can be found.
options.misconception: treats intrinsic toxicity as the whole of risk

options.text: Hazard describes what the substance can do and exposure describes contact with it, so both are needed here.
The site measurements settle it, because a low measured level means the substance is harmless.
options.misconception: ignores intrinsic toxicity when exposure is low

options.text: Both are needed, and their combination is enough without knowing how residents come into contact.
options.misconception: ignores the exposure pathway in the assessment

questions.explanation: Hazard is intrinsic toxicity and exposure is the contact with it, so risk needs both, and here the exposure pathway is closed. No exposure means no risk, and low levels do not make a potent substance harmless.
questions.hint: Risk needs both hazard and exposure.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a combined effect under an independent action model.
questions.stem: Memo: the two solvents in the plume act on different organs, and each sits at 40 percent of the concentration that halves its endpoint.
questions.explanation: Independent action multiplies the fractions without effect, so the combined effect is 1 minus 0.6 times 0.6, giving 0.64 or 64 percent. Adding the two separate effects would double-count the effect.
questions.hint: Combine the fractions without effect, then subtract from one.

options.text: The parent's figure understates the risk, because conversion creates the harmful species from a harmless parent.
options.misconception: treats activation as amplifying an effective dose

options.text: The parent's figure is unaffected, because conversion happens only in animals and not in people.
options.misconception: assumes metabolism differs categorically by species

options.text: The parent's figure overstates the dose reaching the target, because only 30 percent is converted to the active species.
The parent's figure can be used directly, since the active species and the parent act at the same strength.
options.misconception: assumes parent and metabolite share potency

questions.explanation: Conversion to the active species means the parent's measured dose is not the dose causing the effect, so parent figures misstate internal dose. Activation does not multiply an effective dose.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpolate a median lethal dose between two mortality points.

stimulus.body: In a rat feeding study, mortality was 25 percent at 40 mg per kg of body weight and 75 percent at 160 mg per kg. The study recorded the response as approximately linear on a log dose scale between those two points. No confidence interval is given in the summary table.

questions.stem: Using the appendix, how should the LD50 for these rats be reported?

options.text: As 100 mg per kg, the arithmetic mean of 40 and 160, since the median must lie halfway between them.
options.misconception: averages doses arithmetically on a log response

options.text: As 80 mg per kg, the geometric mean of 40 and 160, with a note that the summary gives no interval.
As 40 mg per kg, since that is the lowest dose with any mortality and the most protective figure.
options.misconception: picks the most protective point instead of interpolating

options.text: As 160 mg per kg, since that is the highest dose actually tested and needs no extrapolation.
options.misconception: chooses the highest tested dose to avoid extrapolation

questions.explanation: The geometric mean of 40 and 160 on a log dose scale is the square root of 6400, which is 80 mg per kg. An arithmetic mean ignores the curve's shape, and an end point is not an interpolation.
questions.hint: On a log scale the median is a geometric mean.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compare an observed field decline with a laboratory half-life.

stimulus.body: A 1990 investigation recorded 8 mg per litre of the solvent in pore water below the former drum store. A 2020 sample from the same borehole reads 2 mg per litre. Laboratory testing gives a half-life of 6 years for the compound in that soil.

questions.stem: Using the note, which conclusion is best supported about the solvent's behaviour on site?

options.text: The field fall is much slower than the laboratory half-life predicts, so the compound persists far longer on site.
The field behaviour matches the laboratory half-life exactly, so the 2020 result confirms the test.
options.misconception: reads a two-point decline as confirming the lab rate

options.text: Natural attenuation has worked faster than expected, so the site needs no further investigation.
options.misconception: infers clean-up success from two samples

options.text: The 2020 sample must be wrong, because a halving every six years cannot produce a fourfold fall.
options.misconception: assumes the measurement must be wrong

questions.explanation: A fall from 8 to 2 mg per litre in 30 years is two half-lives, implying a field half-life near 15 years rather than 6. Slow field decay is common, so laboratory rates need site confirmation.
questions.hint: Compare the observed fall with the expected halvings.

questions.hint: It is a population statistic with uncertainty.

options.misconception: prefers modelled output over measurement

options.text: Exposure is the hazard of the substance, since the dose and the danger are the same quantity.
options.misconception: conflates hazard with exposure

options.text: Exposure is what a person actually receives, estimated from measured or modelled contact with the contaminated medium.

questions.explanation: Exposure describes contact between a person and a contaminant, estimated for particular activities and groups. Hazard is a different quantity, and one measurement does not describe every resident.
questions.hint: Exposure is contact, not toxicity.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a summed hazard index for two substances.
questions.stem: Memo: solvent A contributes a toxic unit of 0.7 and solvent B a toxic unit of 0.4 in the plume at the site boundary.
questions.explanation: For the same mechanism the hazard index is the sum of toxic units, so 0.7 plus 0.4 gives 1.1. Above one means the combined dose exceeds the accepted level.
questions.hint: Add the toxic units for a shared mechanism.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise that metabolism may detoxify as well as activate.
questions.stem: Memo: the compound's metabolism removes it as fast as it forms it in laboratory animals, and I need to describe what that means.

options.text: Fast metabolism means the compound is harmless, because the active species never accumulates in the body.
options.misconception: ignores that the active species still forms

options.text: Some compounds are detoxified by the same metabolism that activates others, so the pathway must be identified rather than assumed.
Fast metabolism means the compound is more dangerous, because more active species is produced per hour.
options.misconception: assumes faster metabolism means more activation

options.text: Fast metabolism has no bearing on risk, because only the administered dose matters for the committee.
options.misconception: claims dose alone settles risk

questions.explanation: Metabolism can activate or detoxify a compound, so the direction of the pathway must be established chemically. Neither fast clearance nor fast activation is protective on its own.
questions.hint: Establish whether the pathway activates or detoxifies.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpolate a median lethal dose from two mortality points.
questions.stem: Memo: mortality in the rat study was 25 percent at 30 mg per kg and 75 percent at 90 mg per kg, linear on a log dose scale between them.
questions.explanation: The interpolated LD50 is the geometric mean, so the square root of 30 times 90, which is 2700, gives 51.96 mg per kg. An arithmetic mean of 60 would sit at the wrong point on the curve.
questions.hint: Take the geometric mean of the bracketing doses.
